intro: A silver carp leaps out of the Illinois River and lands in a boat. A pea plant grows wrinkled seeds even though both its parents grew round ones. A bacterium shrugs off a drug that would have killed its great-grandparents. These three scenes look unrelated. They are not. Each one is about the same thing: living things, the instructions inside them, and the pressure of the world around them.

This unit moves from the outside in and then back out again. First, ecosystems: what limits a population, how energy and matter move through a food web, and what happens when a drought, a fire or an invader shakes things up. Next, heredity: how DNA, genes and chromosomes carry instructions from parents to offspring, and why offspring are never exact copies. Finally, evolution: how the variation that heredity creates, meeting the limits that ecosystems impose, changes populations over generations and has produced every species on Earth.

By the end you will be able to read a food web and predict what happens when one species vanishes. You will be able to draw a Punnett square and explain why a trait can hide for a generation. And you will be able to lay out the evidence, from rock layers to finch beaks to DNA, that all living things share one family tree.
bigQuestion: How do the limits of an ecosystem and the instructions inside cells together explain why living things change over generations?

timeline.t: Robert Hooke looks at thin slices of cork through a microscope and names the tiny boxes he sees cells.
Nicolas Steno states that in undisturbed rock layers, deeper layers are older, the law of superposition.
Thomas Malthus argues that populations grow faster than their food supply, an idea Darwin will later borrow.
Charles Darwin sails around the world on HMS Beagle and collects finches in the Galápagos Islands.
Papers by Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace on natural selection are read together at a meeting in London.
Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species, opening with the breeding of pigeons.
Gregor Mendel publishes the results of eight years of pea crosses; almost no one notices.
Three biologists independently rediscover Mendel's ratios and his forgotten paper.
The double-helix structure of DNA is worked out, using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin's lab.
Silver and bighead carp are brought to southern U.S. fish farms; floods let them escape into the Mississippi.
A drought on Daphne Major kills most of the finches; the Grants record a shift toward deeper beaks.
The Human Genome Project announces the essentially complete sequence of human DNA.

test.q: A pond has plenty of water and sunlight, but the insects that frogs eat are scarce. The limiting factor for the frog population is:
test.why: The resource in shortest supply, insects, sets the limit on how many frogs can live there.

test.q: A tick drinks a deer's blood and makes it weaker. This relationship is:
test.why: The tick benefits and the deer is harmed but not killed right away, which is parasitism.
Producers turn light energy into stored sugar, which feeds the rest of the food web.

test.q: If a prairie's plants hold 10,000 energy units, about how many reach the hawks two levels up from the herbivores?
test.why: Roughly 10 percent passes each step: 10,000 to 1,000 to 100 to 10.

test.q: Which best explains why matter does not run out in an ecosystem?
choices: Decomposers recycle atoms from dead material back into the soil and air
test.why: Atoms cycle. Decomposers release nutrients that plants take up again.

test.q: Silver carp spread quickly in the Illinois River mainly because:
choices: They are the largest fish in the river
The predators and diseases that limited them in Asia are absent
The river is warmer than their home rivers
test.why: Without their usual limiting factors, few checks hold the invasive population down.

choices: The instructions in DNA for building one protein
test.why: A gene is one stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. The genome is the whole set.

test.q: Two Rr pea plants are crossed. What share of offspring is expected to show the recessive wrinkled trait?
test.why: The Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Only rr shows the recessive trait.

test.q: Which statement about sexual reproduction is true?
choices: Offspring are exact copies of one parent
It mixes chromosomes from two parents and creates variation
It needs no egg or sperm
test.why: Each parent gives half the chromosomes, in random combinations, so offspring vary.

test.q: A mutation in which cell could be passed to the next generation?
test.why: Only mutations in egg or sperm cells are inherited.

test.q: Why is the sickle cell allele common where malaria is widespread?
choices: Carriers with one copy survive malaria better
test.why: Having one copy protects against severe malaria, so selection keeps the allele common despite its cost.

test.q: Which order of first appearance matches the fossil record from bottom to top?
test.why: The lowest layers hold only microbes; fish appear far above, and mammals near the top.

test.q: After the 1977 drought, the average beak of Daphne Major finches was deeper. This happened because:
choices: Each finch grew a deeper beak to crack seeds
Deep-beaked finches survived and passed on their genes more than others
The finches practiced on hard seeds
The drought changed the finches' DNA directly
test.why: Individuals did not change. The population shifted because survival depended on a heritable trait.

test.q: Bacteria that survive a course of antibiotics are the ones that:
choices: Were never exposed to the drug
Already carried a mutation that let them resist
test.why: The drug selects for resistant cells that existed before treatment; their descendants take over.

test.q: Humans and chimpanzees are best described as:
choices: Unrelated species that happen to look alike
Cousins that share a common ancestor from millions of years ago
test.why: Neither came from the other. Both descend from an ape ancestor that lived roughly six or seven million years ago.

write.prompt: Silver carp have spread through the Illinois River and threaten Lake Michigan. Make a claim: should Illinois keep spending on electric barriers, netting and marketing the fish as food, or accept the carp as a permanent part of the river? Support it with evidence from this unit about limiting factors, food webs, biodiversity and how populations change, and explain your reasoning.

Use at least three pieces of evidence: for example, what carp eat, how the 10 percent rule affects native fish, and why the carp population grew so fast here.
Explain your reasoning: connect each piece of evidence to your claim with a because.
Consider what selection might do to the carp themselves over many generations, and whether that changes your answer.
Give the other side a fair hearing: what is the strongest argument against your claim, and why does your claim still hold?

title: Ecosystems, Heredity and Evolution

chapters.title: Ecosystems and Populations
chapters.bigQuestion: What decides how many living things a place can hold, and what happens when something new arrives?

story.title: The Fish That Jumped Into the Boat
story.kicker: On the Illinois River, a motor's hum can fill the air with flying fish.
paragraphs: Maya's uncle eases the boat away from the ramp near Havana, Illinois. The Illinois River is wide and brown here. He pushes the throttle. The motor hums. Then the water in front of them explodes. Silver fish, some as long as her arm, leap out of the river. They fly higher than her head. One slams into the side of the boat. Another lands, flopping, at her feet.

Her uncle cuts the motor and laughs, but he is not happy. "Silver carp," he says. "They jump when a motor scares them. Twenty years ago you never saw one here." He holds the fish up. It has a low, forward-set eye and a big silver body. It did not come from Illinois. It did not come from anywhere in North America.

Silver carp and their cousins, bighead carp, were brought to the southern United States in the 1970s. Fish farms wanted them to eat algae and clean their ponds. Floods let some escape into the Mississippi River. From there they swam north, up the Illinois River, toward Chicago and Lake Michigan. They eat tiny floating plankton, the same food that young native fish need.

Today biologists net, count and track these carp all along the river. Electric barriers near Romeoville, in the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, are meant to keep them out of the Great Lakes. Restaurants are learning to cook them. Illinois even gave the fish a new market name, copi, to get more people to eat them.

Maya looks at the fish at her feet. It is just a fish, doing what fish do: eating and making more fish. So why is it a problem? Her uncle points at the water. "Everything down there is connected," he says. "Change one thing, and you change the whole river."
story.think: The carp is only eating plankton. Why might that hurt bass, bluegill and other native fish that do not eat plankton at all?

lessons.title: Counting a Population
lessons.mainIdea: A population is all the members of one species in one place, and it can only grow as far as its resources allow.
reading: Picture a pond in a Chicago park in early summer. Frogs call from the edges. If you counted every bullfrog in that pond, you would have measured a *population*: all the individuals of one species living in one place at one time. The pond also has a population of bluegill, a population of cattails and a population of mosquitoes. Together, all of them and the water, mud and sunlight make an ecosystem.

No population can grow forever. Each frog needs food, water, space and a place to lay eggs. These are *resources*. When resources are plentiful, a population grows fast. A pair of frogs can produce thousands of eggs. When the pond gets crowded, food runs short and growth slows. Some frogs starve, and fewer eggs hatch.

Scientists call the largest population a place can support over time its *carrying capacity*. The resource that runs out first sets that limit. Ecologists call it a *limiting factor*. For pond frogs it might be insects to eat. For prairie plants it might be water in a dry August. For nesting birds it might be tree holes. Find the limiting factor, and you can often predict how a population will change.

words.d: all the individuals of one species living in one place at one time
the things living things need to survive, such as food, water, space and shelter
the largest population that a place can support over time
the resource or condition that runs out first and stops a population from growing

look.title: The Empty Bird Feeder
look.text: A family in Peoria fills a bird feeder every day all winter. By February, twenty cardinals visit each morning. In March the family moves away. The feeder stays empty. By April only four cardinals come to the yard. Nothing else in the neighborhood changed.
look.prompt: What was the limiting factor for the cardinal population in that yard, and what evidence tells you so?

check.q: Which of these is a population?
choices: All the bullfrogs in one pond
All the animals in one pond
check.why: A population is one species in one place. Many species together are a community, not a population.

check.q: A pond has plenty of insects, water and space, but only three logs where frogs can hide. What is the limiting factor?
check.why: The resource in shortest supply limits the population. Here that is shelter, not food or water.

check.q: What most likely happens to a deer population that has reached carrying capacity?
choices: It stops growing and stays near the same size
check.why: At carrying capacity, births and deaths roughly balance, so the population levels off.

lessons.title: Competition and Predation
lessons.mainIdea: Living things compete for the same resources, and predators and prey keep each other's numbers in check.
reading: Two oak seedlings sprout side by side in a forest preserve. Both need light, water and soil minerals. There is not enough for both to grow tall. This is *competition*: two or more living things trying to use the same limited resource. The seedling that grows a little faster shades the other. The slower one dies. Competition happens within a species and between species.

Now watch a red-tailed hawk drop onto a field mouse. The hawk is a *predator*, an animal that hunts and eats other animals. The mouse is its *prey*. Predation is not cruelty; it is how the hawk gets energy. It also shapes the mouse population. When mice are plentiful, hawks raise more chicks. When hawks are plentiful, mice become scarce, and then some hawks go hungry.

Ecologists have tracked predators and prey for decades. The numbers often rise and fall in linked waves. Prey numbers climb first. Predator numbers climb a little later. Then prey numbers crash, and predators follow. The pattern is evidence that the two populations control each other. Remove the predator, and prey can boom until they eat their food supply bare.

words.d: when two or more living things try to use the same limited resource
an animal that hunts and eats other animals
an animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator

look.title: Two Weeds, One Pot
look.text: A student plants ten radish seeds in one small pot and ten in a second pot, then thins the second pot to two seedlings. Both pots get the same light and water. After three weeks the crowded pot has ten thin, pale plants about 4 cm tall. The thinned pot has two thick, dark green plants about 12 cm tall.
look.prompt: What were the radishes in the crowded pot competing for, and how do you know competition happened?

check.q: Two squirrels chase each other away from the same pile of acorns. This is an example of:
check.why: Both squirrels want the same limited food. That is competition, not predation, since neither eats the other.

check.q: If hunters removed every coyote from a county, what would you predict for the rabbit population at first?
choices: It would stay exactly the same
check.why: With no predator, more rabbits survive and breed. Later, food may run short and the boom may crash.

check.q: In records of predators and prey, predator numbers usually rise:
choices: A little after prey numbers rise
At the same moment prey numbers fall
check.why: Predators need more food before they can raise more young, so their peak comes after the prey peak.

lessons.title: Partners and Parasites
lessons.mainIdea: Species can help each other, use each other, or harm each other, and each kind of relationship shapes an ecosystem.
reading: A bumblebee lands on a purple coneflower in an Illinois prairie. The bee drinks sugary nectar. Pollen sticks to its fuzzy body and rides to the next flower, letting the plant make seeds. Both partners gain. Ecologists call this *mutualism*. Clownfish and sea anemones, and the bacteria in your own gut that help you digest food, are also mutualists.

Not every close relationship is fair. A tick clings to a deer and drinks its blood. The tick gains; the deer loses blood and may get sick. This is *parasitism*. A parasite lives on or in another organism, called the host, and harms it, usually without killing it right away. Tapeworms, fleas and the fungus that causes athlete's foot are parasites.

Sometimes one partner gains and the other is not affected much. A barnacle riding on a whale gets a free trip to food-rich water; the whale barely notices. Scientists call that commensalism. Together, mutualism, parasitism, competition and predation are the threads that tie an ecosystem together. Pull one thread, and others move.

words.d: a relationship between two species in which both gain something
a relationship in which one organism lives on or in another and harms it
the organism that a parasite lives on or in

look.title: Darwin's Tangled Bank
look.text: It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us.
look.cite: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species, 1859
look.prompt: Darwin says the plants, birds, insects and worms are dependent on each other. Name two relationships from this lesson that could connect them.

check.q: A bee gets nectar and a flower gets pollinated. This relationship is:
check.why: Both the bee and the flower gain, which is the definition of mutualism.

check.q: Which is the best example of a parasite?
choices: A hawk that eats a mouse
A tapeworm living in a dog's intestine
check.why: The tapeworm lives inside its host and harms it slowly without killing it right away.

check.q: Which statement about commensalism is correct?
choices: One species gains and the other is not much affected
check.why: In commensalism one partner benefits while the other is barely affected, like a barnacle on a whale.

sections.title: Energy and Matter on the Move

lessons.title: Sunlight Into Sugar
lessons.mainIdea: Plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and that sugar feeds almost every living thing.
reading: Put a leaf under the site's microscope and you will see tiny green dots packed inside the cells. These are chloroplasts. Inside them, *photosynthesis* happens. The plant takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny pores and water from the soil through its roots. Using the energy of sunlight, it links those simple molecules into sugar. Oxygen is released as a leftover.

That sugar is stored chemical energy. The plant uses some of it to grow. The rest is stored in leaves, stems, roots and seeds. When a rabbit eats clover, it takes in that stored energy. When a fox eats the rabbit, the energy moves again. Nearly all the energy in an ecosystem entered it as sunlight caught by a *producer*, an organism that makes its own food.

You can test this. Put a water plant like elodea in a jar of water in bright light. Bubbles rise from the leaves. In the dark, the bubbling stops. The bubbles are oxygen, released only when light drives photosynthesis. In the 1770s, Jan Ingenhousz did a version of this experiment and showed that green plants give off oxygen only in light.

Photosynthesis also explains the air you breathe. About 21 percent of the air is oxygen, almost all of it made by producers over billions of years. Carbon dioxide is far rarer, about 0.04 percent, yet every gram of sugar in every plant was built from it.

words.d: the process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water
an organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
the green part of a plant cell where photosynthesis happens

look.title: What Is in Dry Air
look.prompt: Carbon dioxide is a tiny part of the air. Why does it matter so much to plants, and what would happen to photosynthesis if it were gone?

check.q: Which ingredients does a plant use to make sugar in photosynthesis?
choices: Carbon dioxide, water and light energy
check.why: Photosynthesis links carbon dioxide and water into sugar using light energy, and oxygen is released.

check.q: An elodea plant in a jar stops bubbling when the lamp is turned off. What does this show?
choices: The plant is now making sugar faster
The water ran out of carbon dioxide
check.why: The bubbles are oxygen from photosynthesis, and they stop without light because the process needs light energy.

check.q: Where did the energy in a fox's meal originally come from?
check.why: The rabbit ate plants, and the plants stored energy from sunlight. Energy enters most ecosystems as light.

lessons.title: Food Webs and the Ten Percent Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Energy flows one way through a food web, and only a small share passes from each level to the next.
reading: A food chain is a simple line: grass to grasshopper to sparrow to hawk. Real ecosystems are messier. The sparrow also eats seeds. The hawk also eats snakes. A *food web* is a diagram of many linked chains that shows who eats whom in a whole community. Arrows point in the direction the energy moves, from the eaten to the eater.

Every organism in a web sits at a level. Producers are the first level. Animals that eat producers are herbivores, the second level. Animals that eat herbivores are the third, and so on. An organism that eats other organisms is a *consumer*. Some consumers, like raccoons and people, eat at several levels.

Energy is lost at every step. A grasshopper uses most of the energy from the grass it eats just to move, breathe and stay alive. That energy leaves as heat. Only about 10 percent gets stored in the grasshopper's body where a sparrow can get it. The same thing happens at each level. This is why a prairie can feed millions of insects, thousands of birds and only a few dozen hawks.

The pattern is called an energy pyramid. It explains something you can see everywhere: big predators are rare. It also explains why a food web rarely has more than four or five levels. By the fifth level there is almost no energy left to pass along.

words.d: a diagram of linked food chains that shows who eats whom in a community
an organism that gets energy by eating other organisms
a diagram showing that each feeding level holds only about a tenth of the energy of the level below it

look.title: Energy Passed Up a Prairie Food Web
look.cite: standard textbook rule of thumb: roughly 10 percent passes to each next level
look.prompt: Suppose people planted a crop that cut the prairie's grass energy in half. Using the pattern, about how much energy would reach the hawks?

check.q: In a food web, which way do the arrows point?
choices: From the eater to the eaten
From the eaten to the eater
From big animals to small animals
check.why: Arrows show where the energy goes, so they point from the food to the organism that eats it.

check.q: About how much of the energy in grass ends up stored in the grasshoppers that eat it?
check.why: Most energy is used for living and lost as heat. Only roughly a tenth is stored at the next level.

check.q: Why are top predators like hawks so rare compared with insects?
choices: Hawks do not need much energy
Little energy is left by the top of the food web
check.why: Energy shrinks at each level, so there is only enough left to support a few animals at the top.

lessons.title: Decomposers Close the Loop
lessons.mainIdea: Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat, but matter cycles, and decomposers are what keep it cycling.
reading: Turn over a rotting log in a forest preserve. The wood is soft and crumbling. Threads of white fungus run through it. Beetles, worms and millions of bacteria are at work. These are *decomposers*: organisms that break dead material into simple substances. Without them, every fallen leaf and dead animal would pile up forever, and the minerals locked inside would never get back to the soil.

This points to a big difference between energy and matter. Energy moves one way. It enters as sunlight, passes up the food web, and leaves as heat. It is not recycled. Matter is different. The carbon atom in a leaf becomes part of a caterpillar, then a bird, then a decomposer, then carbon dioxide in the air, then a new leaf. Atoms are used over and over. This is *cycling* of matter.

The carbon cycle is the easiest to see. Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air. Animals eat plants and breathe out carbon dioxide. Decomposers release it as they rot dead things. Nitrogen and water cycle too. Rain falls, plants drink it, animals drink it, and it evaporates back to the sky. The same water has been through countless living things.

Illinois farmers rely on these cycles. Rich prairie soil formed over thousands of years as decomposers broke down dead grasses and roots. That dark soil holds nutrients that corn and soybeans now use. Take away the decomposers, and the soil would stop being renewed.

words.d: an organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks dead material into simple substances
the movement of matter, such as carbon or water, around and around through an ecosystem

look.title: The Leaf Bag Experiment
look.text: A class fills two mesh bags with 100 grams of dry oak leaves each. One bag is buried in moist forest soil. The other is sealed in a dry, sterile jar. After six months they weigh the leaves again. The buried leaves weigh 40 grams and are dark, soft and full of tiny roots and fungus threads. The jar leaves still weigh 100 grams and look the same.
look.prompt: Where did the missing 60 grams from the buried bag go? What does the jar tell you about what decomposers need?

check.q: Which is the best example of a decomposer?
choices: A fungus growing on a dead log
check.why: Fungi break dead material down into simple substances that return to the soil.

check.q: Which statement is true?
choices: Both energy and matter are recycled in an ecosystem
Energy is recycled, but matter is lost
Matter is recycled, but energy flows through and leaves as heat
Neither energy nor matter moves in an ecosystem
check.why: Atoms cycle again and again, but energy enters as sunlight and eventually leaves as heat.

check.q: If all decomposers in a forest vanished, what would happen over many years?
choices: Dead material would pile up and soil nutrients would run low
The forest would get more sunlight
check.why: Decomposers return nutrients from dead things to the soil. Without them, nutrients stay locked in dead material.

lessons.title: Why Variety Matters
lessons.mainIdea: Biodiversity, the variety of living things in a place, makes an ecosystem stronger and gives people services they cannot easily replace.
reading: Walk a restored prairie at the Midewin National Tallgrass Prairie southwest of Chicago. In one square meter you may find a dozen kinds of grass and flower. Beneath them are insects, spiders, fungi and bacteria by the thousands. This variety is *biodiversity*: the number of different species in a place and the variety within each species.

Why care about variety? Think of a bank with many kinds of savings. If one loses value, others still hold. A prairie with thirty plant species can survive a dry summer better than a field of one crop. Some species will do poorly, but others will thrive and hold the soil. A monoculture, a field of just one kind, has no backup plan.

Ecosystems also do work for people for free. Wetlands soak up floodwater. Forests filter drinking water and hold hillsides in place. Bees and other insects pollinate the apple and pumpkin crops of Illinois. Decomposers build soil. Scientists call these *ecosystem services*. When biodiversity falls, these services get weaker, and replacing them with machines is costly or impossible.

words.d: the variety of living things in a place, counted as species and as differences within species
useful things an ecosystem does for people, like cleaning water, pollinating crops and building soil
a field or area with only one kind of plant growing in it

look.title: Two Fields in a Dry August
look.text: Two neighboring fields in central Illinois get the same rain. Field A is planted with one variety of corn. Field B is a restored prairie with more than forty species of grasses and flowers. A drought hits in August. In Field A, nearly every plant wilts and the soil cracks. In Field B, some plants wilt, but deep-rooted species stay green and the soil stays covered.
look.prompt: Why did Field B hold up better? What ecosystem service did its biodiversity protect?

check.q: Biodiversity means:
choices: The number of animals in a zoo
The variety of living things in a place
The size of the largest species
check.why: Biodiversity measures how many different kinds of living things there are and how varied they are.

check.q: Which is an ecosystem service?
check.why: Flood control by wetlands is work an ecosystem does for people for free.

check.q: Why might a prairie with many species survive drought better than a single-crop field?
choices: All prairie plants have shallow roots
Prairie plants do not need water
Some species will tolerate drought even if others fail
check.why: With many species, at least some are likely to survive hard conditions and keep the system working.

lessons.title: When an Invader Arrives
lessons.mainIdea: A species carried to a new place can spread fast if nothing there eats it or competes with it, and it can push out native species.
reading: Silver carp did not evolve on the Illinois River. Back home in Asia, their eggs and young are eaten by many predators, and diseases keep their numbers down. In the Mississippi basin, few of those checks exist. A single female can release hundreds of thousands of eggs. With little to stop them, the carp population exploded. A species that spreads in a new place and causes harm is an *invasive species*.

The carp cause harm in a quiet way. They filter plankton, the tiny floating organisms at the base of the river's food web. Nearly every native fish eats plankton when it is young. When carp take that food, fewer young bass, crappie and bluegill survive. This is competition on a huge scale. In some stretches of the Illinois River, biologists have found that carp make up a large share of all the fish by weight.

Illinois is not alone. Zebra mussels arrived in the Great Lakes in ship ballast water in the 1980s and now coat pipes and rocks. Emerald ash borer beetles have killed millions of ash trees across the state. Garlic mustard shades out spring wildflowers in forest preserves. In each case the invader lacked the predators, parasites and competitors that limited it at home.

Fighting invaders takes many tools. For the carp, crews use nets, electric barriers in the canal, and a push to turn the fish into food. None of these will remove every carp. The goal is to keep the population low enough that native fish can recover and to keep the carp out of Lake Michigan.

words.d: a species that spreads in a place where it did not live before and harms the ecosystem there
tiny organisms that drift in water and feed young fish and many other animals
a species that has lived in a place for a very long time and fits its ecosystem

look.title: Why Here and Not There
look.text: In its home rivers in China, a silver carp population stays fairly steady. Eggs are eaten by dozens of fish species. Young carp are hunted by birds and larger fish. Local parasites weaken adults. In the Illinois River, the same species faces few egg predators and few parasites. Within twenty years of arriving, its numbers grew enormously.
look.prompt: Using the ideas of limiting factors and predation, explain why the same fish behaves so differently in the two rivers.

check.q: Why do invasive species often grow so fast in a new place?
choices: They need less food than native species
The predators and diseases that limited them at home are missing
New places always have more sunlight
They are always bigger than native species
check.why: Without their usual predators, parasites and competitors, few limiting factors hold the population down.

check.q: How do silver carp harm native fish in the Illinois River?
choices: They compete for the plankton that young native fish need
They block sunlight from reaching plants
check.why: Carp filter huge amounts of plankton, the food most native fish depend on when young.

check.q: Which is an example of an invasive species in Illinois?
check.why: The emerald ash borer came from Asia and has killed millions of native ash trees.

lessons.title: Drought, Fire and Recovery
lessons.mainIdea: Disturbances like drought and fire can knock an ecosystem down, and its resilience decides how well it bounces back.
reading: In the summer of 2012, much of Illinois went weeks without real rain. Corn leaves curled. Ponds shrank to mud. Fish died in shallow water that got too warm and held too little oxygen. A *disturbance* is any event that changes an ecosystem quickly. Drought, flood, fire, storms and the arrival of an invader are all disturbances.

Fire sounds like pure destruction, but on a prairie it is an old friend. Before farms, lightning and Native American land managers set fires that swept the tallgrass every few years. Prairie plants grow from deep roots and buds below the soil, so they survive. Fire clears dead stems and kills young trees that would shade out the grass. Today, land managers at forest preserves set careful controlled burns for the same reason.

*Resilience* is an ecosystem's ability to recover after a disturbance. A prairie with many species and deep roots is resilient to fire and drought. A lawn of one grass type is not. Resilience has limits. If fires come too often, or a drought lasts years, or an invader never leaves, an ecosystem can tip into a different state and stay there. A shallow lake choked with algae may not turn clear again on its own.

Scientists measure resilience by tracking a place over time. They count species before and after a disturbance and record how long recovery takes. That evidence helps decide where to protect land, where to burn, and when to step in.

words.d: an event like drought, fire or flood that changes an ecosystem quickly
the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance
a fire that land managers set on purpose, under safe conditions, to help a prairie or forest

look.title: After the Burn
look.text: A land manager burns half of a prairie in March and leaves the other half alone. In June, the burned half is a thick sea of green grass and flowers with almost no young trees. The unburned half is shorter, with a mat of dead stems and dozens of small oak and elm seedlings poking through.
look.prompt: What evidence here shows the prairie is resilient to fire? What might the unburned half look like in twenty years if it is never burned?

check.q: Which is a disturbance to an ecosystem?
choices: A slow change in a bird's beak over centuries
A drought that dries up a pond
check.why: Drought changes the ecosystem quickly. The other choices are normal, ongoing parts of ecosystem life.

check.q: Why does a prairie survive fire so well?
choices: Prairie plants regrow from deep roots and buried buds
Fire adds water to the soil
check.why: The parts above ground burn, but the living roots and buds below the soil send up new growth.

check.q: Which ecosystem is probably the most resilient to a dry summer?
choices: A lawn of one grass species
A parking lot planter with one shrub
A prairie with forty plant species and deep roots
check.why: Many species with deep roots give the prairie more ways to survive and recover.

lessons.title: Define the Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Before designing a fix, engineers and ecologists state exactly what must be protected, what limits the solution, and how success will be measured.
reading: Suppose your class is asked to help a small creek in your town. Fish have disappeared. Where do you start? Engineers begin by defining the problem. What exactly went wrong? Perhaps a new parking lot sends muddy water into the creek after every storm. Mud buries the gravel where fish lay eggs. Now the problem is clear: too much sediment reaching the creek.

Next come the *criteria*: what a good solution must do. It must cut the mud reaching the creek. It must not flood the parking lot. Then come the *constraints*: the limits. There is a budget. The lot must stay open. The fix must be built by spring. A solution that fails a constraint is not a real option, no matter how clever.

Finally, decide how you will know it worked. Ecologists set a measurable goal, like the amount of mud in a water sample or the number of fish counted next summer. Without a measurement, you can only guess. Defining the problem well is often half the job.

words.d: the things a solution must do to count as a success
the limits on a solution, such as cost, time, space or safety
mud, sand and silt carried by water and dropped where the water slows

look.title: The Muddy Creek
look.text: After each rainstorm, students measure how cloudy the creek water is by lowering a white disk on a string and recording the depth at which it disappears. In April, before a new parking lot was paved upstream, the disk vanished at about 60 cm. In June, after the lot opened, it vanishes at about 15 cm after storms. Fish nests in the gravel are covered with silt.
look.prompt: State the problem in one sentence. Then write one criterion and one constraint for a solution.

check.q: What is the first step in designing a solution to an ecosystem problem?
check.why: Engineers and ecologists first pin down exactly what is wrong before choosing a fix.

check.q: "The fix must cost less than 5,000 dollars" is an example of a:
check.why: A constraint is a limit on the solution. Cost, time and space are common constraints.

check.q: Why should a plan include a measurable goal?
choices: So the plan gets built faster
So you can tell whether the solution actually worked
check.why: Without a measurement, you cannot compare before and after or know if the fix succeeded.

lessons.title: Compare, Test and Choose
lessons.mainIdea: Good ecosystem solutions come from comparing several ideas against the criteria, testing them on a small scale, and weighing trade-offs.
reading: With the muddy creek problem defined, the class brainstorms. One group wants a strip of native plants between the lot and the creek. Roots slow the water and trap mud. Another group wants a small basin that catches storm water. A third wants to replace part of the lot with pavement that lets rain soak through. None of these is obviously best. Each must be scored against the criteria and constraints.

Engineers then *test* on a small scale. The class builds three tray models with a sloped surface, sprinkles water from a can, and measures how much soil washes into a cup at the bottom. The plant strip cuts the mud by about half. The basin catches nearly all of it but overflows in a heavy pour. The porous pavement works but costs the most.

Every choice has a *trade-off*: something you give up to get something else. The basin takes space. The plant strip needs years to grow. Porous pavement needs cleaning. Sometimes the best answer combines ideas. The class might pick a plant strip plus a small basin and plan to measure creek clarity every month to see if fish come back.

This is how real projects go. When Illinois planned electric barriers against the carp, engineers compared a barrier with dams, locks and nets, weighed cost and shipping traffic, and then monitored the results for years. Protecting an ecosystem is not one decision. It is a cycle of trying, measuring and improving.

words.d: to try a solution in a controlled way and measure how well it works
something you give up in order to gain something else
a small or simplified version of something used to test ideas

look.title: Tray Model Results
look.unit: grams of soil in the cup, class model
look.cite: classroom model, made-up example for practice
look.prompt: The basin caught the most soil but overflowed in a hard rain and takes the most space. Which fix or combination would you choose, and what trade-off are you accepting?

check.q: Why do engineers test ideas with small models first?
choices: Models are always exactly like the real thing
Testing on a small scale is cheaper and safer than building the real thing right away
Real tests are against the rules
check.why: Small tests give evidence about what works before money and time go into the full project.

check.q: A catch basin stops nearly all mud but takes up parking spaces. The lost spaces are a:
check.why: A trade-off is what you give up, here parking space, to gain something else, here clean water.

check.q: After a solution is built, what should happen next?
choices: Keep measuring to see if it works and improve it
check.why: Protecting an ecosystem is a cycle. Measuring after the fix shows whether it met the goal.

review.why: One species in one place is a population.

review.q: A meadow has plenty of grass and water but very few places for rabbits to hide from hawks. The limiting factor for rabbits is most likely:
review.why: The resource in shortest supply, hiding places, limits how many rabbits can survive.

review.q: Which relationship helps both species?
choices: Two oak seedlings in one spot
review.why: The bee gets nectar and the flower gets pollinated, so it is mutualism.

review.q: In photosynthesis, a plant releases:
review.why: Oxygen is the leftover gas released when plants build sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

review.q: A food web has 10,000 energy units in its plants. About how many units reach the animals that eat the herbivores?
review.why: About 10 percent passes each level: 10,000 to about 1,000 in herbivores, then about 100 in their predators.

review.q: Which statement about energy and matter in an ecosystem is correct?
choices: Matter cycles; energy flows through and leaves as heat
Energy cycles; matter is used up
review.why: Atoms are reused again and again, while energy enters as light and leaves as heat.

review.q: Silver carp harm the Illinois River mainly because they:
choices: Compete for plankton with young native fish
Add too much oxygen to the water

review.why: Resilience is the ability to recover after a disturbance such as fire.

chapters.title: Heredity and Genes
chapters.bigQuestion: How do instructions for building a living thing pass from parents to offspring, and why are offspring never exact copies?

story.title: The Monk Who Counted Peas
story.kicker: In a monastery garden, one patient man found the rules of heredity in thousands of pea plants.
paragraphs: In 1856, in the town of Brno in what is now the Czech Republic, a monk named Gregor Mendel walked out to a small garden beside the monastery wall. He had been a physics student. He liked numbers. He had a question that farmers had asked for centuries: why does a child look like its parents, and why does it sometimes not?

Mendel chose the garden pea. Peas are easy to grow, and each flower usually fertilizes itself, so a plant's offspring stay true year after year. He picked traits that came in two clear forms with nothing in between: round or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green seeds, tall or short stems, purple or white flowers. Then he did something almost no one had done before. He counted.

He crossed a true-breeding round-seeded plant with a true-breeding wrinkled one, brushing pollen from one flower onto another by hand. Every seed in the next generation was round. The wrinkled form had vanished. Then he let those plants fertilize themselves. Wrinkled seeds came back: 1,850 of them among 5,474 round ones. Almost exactly one in four.

He tried yellow and green, tall and short, one trait after another. The same pattern appeared every time: the hidden form disappeared for one generation, then returned in about one quarter of the next. Over eight years he grew and counted about 28,000 plants. In 1866 he published his results, and hardly anyone read them.

Mendel died in 1884, still mostly unknown as a scientist. In 1900, three biologists working separately found the same three-to-one ratio and then found Mendel's paper. The rules he uncovered in that garden are now the foundation of genetics. He had never seen a chromosome or a gene. He had only counted, carefully, and trusted the numbers.
story.think: Mendel's wrinkled trait vanished for one generation and then came back in one quarter of the plants. What might that tell you about how the instructions for a trait are stored and passed on?

lessons.title: Chromosomes and DNA
lessons.mainIdea: Every cell carries its instructions as DNA, packed into chromosomes, and each species has its own set.
reading: Look at a dividing onion root cell under the site's microscope at high power. Inside the nucleus, dark threads appear, line up and pull apart. These threads are *chromosomes*. Each one is a tightly coiled strand of *DNA*, a long molecule shaped like a twisted ladder. The rungs of the ladder are pairs of four chemical bases, usually written A, T, C and G. The order of those letters is the instruction.

Your body cells each hold 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. One chromosome of each pair came from your mother and one from your father. Dogs have 78. Fruit flies have 8. The pea plants Mendel grew have 14. The number does not measure how complex an organism is; it is just how that species packages its DNA.

The instructions are astonishingly long. All the DNA in one human cell holds about 3 billion base pairs. Stretched out, it would be about 2 meters long, yet it fits inside a nucleus far too small to see without a microscope. When a cell divides, it copies every chromosome first, so each new cell gets a full set.

words.d: a tightly coiled strand of DNA inside a cell's nucleus that carries many genes
the long twisted-ladder molecule whose sequence of bases holds the instructions for a living thing
the part of a cell that holds the chromosomes

look.title: Chromosome Counts in Body Cells
look.prompt: A dog has more chromosomes than a human. Does that mean a dog is more complex? What does the count actually tell you?

check.q: Chromosomes are made of:
check.why: Each chromosome is one long DNA molecule coiled up tightly with proteins.

check.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human body cell?
check.why: Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent.

check.q: What carries the actual instruction in DNA?
choices: The order of the four bases
check.why: The sequence of A, T, C and G is the code. Different orders mean different instructions.

lessons.title: Genes Build Proteins
lessons.mainIdea: A gene is a stretch of DNA that tells a cell how to build one protein, and proteins do the work that gives an organism its traits.
reading: A chromosome is like a long book. A *gene* is one recipe in that book: a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for building one *protein*. Proteins are the working molecules of a cell. Some are building blocks, like the collagen in your skin and the keratin in your hair. Some are tools, like the enzymes that break down your lunch. Some carry signals, like insulin.

Here is how the recipe becomes a trait. A cell reads a gene and links together a chain of small units called amino acids in the order the gene spells out. The chain folds into a protein with a specific shape. That shape decides what the protein can do. A pea plant with a working gene for a starch-building enzyme makes round seeds. If that enzyme does not form correctly, the seed dries out wrinkled. Mendel's round and wrinkled traits come down to one protein.

Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes. Your eye color, your blood type, whether you can digest milk as an adult, and how your body handles some medicines all trace back to which versions of certain genes you carry and which proteins they build. Many traits, like height, depend on hundreds of genes working together plus food and environment.

words.d: a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for building one protein
a working molecule built by a cell from a gene's instructions; proteins build structures and do jobs in the body
a feature of an organism, like seed shape or eye color
a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in a living thing

look.title: One Broken Recipe
look.text: Two pea seeds sit on the bench. One is smooth and round. One is shrunken and wrinkled. Inside the round seed, an enzyme has turned sugar into starch, which holds water well. Inside the wrinkled seed, the gene for that enzyme has a change in it. The enzyme never forms properly. Less starch is made, more water is lost as the seed dries, and the seed coat collapses.
look.prompt: Trace the chain from gene to trait for the wrinkled seed. Which step changed first, and which step is the trait you can see?

check.q: A gene is best described as:
choices: The instructions for building one protein
check.why: A gene is one stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. A chromosome holds many genes.

check.q: Which of these is a protein?
check.why: Enzymes are proteins. They are built from amino acids using a gene's instructions.

check.q: Why does a change in a gene often change a trait?
choices: Because genes are made of protein
Because the protein it builds may change shape and stop working
Because the cell loses its nucleus
check.why: The protein's shape depends on the gene's sequence, and shape decides what the protein can do.

lessons.title: Dominant and Recessive
lessons.mainIdea: Each organism carries two copies of most genes, and a dominant version can hide a recessive one for a generation.
reading: Mendel's peas carried a secret he could not see. Each plant has two copies of the gene for seed shape, one on each chromosome of a pair. Different versions of a gene are called *alleles*. Call the round allele R and the wrinkled allele r. A plant with two R alleles, RR, makes round seeds. A plant with rr makes wrinkled seeds. A plant with Rr makes round seeds too, because one working enzyme gene is enough.

The allele that shows even when only one copy is present is *dominant*. The one that hides is *recessive*. When Mendel crossed RR with rr, every offspring got one R and one r. All were Rr, and all were round. The wrinkled allele had not vanished. It was riding along, hidden.

When Rr plants fertilized themselves, each parent passed on either R or r, at random. The offspring could be RR, Rr, rR or rr, each equally likely. Three of those four combinations contain at least one R and look round. One is rr and looks wrinkled. Three to one. Mendel's ratio was not magic. It was two alleles per plant, one passed on by each parent, sorted by chance.

words.d: one version of a gene; for example, the round allele or the wrinkled allele for seed shape
an allele that shows its trait even when only one copy is present
an allele whose trait shows only when both copies are that allele

look.title: Mendel's Counts in the Second Generation
look.cite: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybrids, 1866
look.prompt: Divide the larger number by the smaller in each pair. What ratio do you get? Why is it close to, but not exactly, three to one?

check.q: A pea plant with alleles Rr makes round seeds. This shows that the round allele is:
check.why: A dominant allele shows its trait even when paired with a different allele.

check.q: What must a plant's alleles be if it makes wrinkled seeds?
check.why: The recessive trait appears only when both copies are the recessive allele.

check.q: Why did the wrinkled trait disappear in Mendel's first generation and return in the second?
choices: The wrinkled allele was hidden by the dominant allele and then paired up again by chance
The plants forgot how to be wrinkled
The wrinkled allele was destroyed and then rebuilt
check.why: All first-generation plants were Rr and looked round. Their offspring could be rr, which shows the hidden trait.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Reproduce
lessons.mainIdea: Asexual reproduction copies one parent exactly, while sexual reproduction mixes genes from two parents and creates variation.
reading: Snap a stem off a spider plant, put it in water, and roots grow. The new plant is a copy of the old one, with identical DNA. This is *asexual reproduction*: one parent, no mixing, offspring that are clones. Bacteria split in two this way. So do hydras, some lizards and many plants. It is fast, and it works well when conditions are stable.

Most animals and plants also reproduce sexually. In *sexual reproduction*, each parent makes special cells, egg or sperm in animals, that carry only one chromosome from each pair. In humans that is 23. When egg and sperm join, the offspring gets 46: half from each parent. Which chromosome of each pair ends up in a given egg or sperm is random, so every child of the same parents gets a different mix.

That mixing creates *variation*, differences among individuals. Two siblings share parents but not the same combination of alleles. Variation is why a family's children look alike but never identical, unless they are identical twins from one fertilized egg. It also matters for survival. If a new disease strikes, a population with variation is more likely to include some individuals that resist it.

words.d: reproduction from one parent that makes offspring with the same DNA as the parent
reproduction in which two parents each give half the chromosomes, making offspring with a new mix
differences among individuals of the same species

look.title: The Potato Blight
look.text: In the 1840s most of Ireland's potatoes were one variety, grown by planting pieces of last year's potatoes rather than seeds. Every plant was a clone with the same DNA. When a fungus-like disease arrived, it spread through fields with almost nothing to slow it, and the harvests failed for several years in a row.
look.prompt: Why was a crop of clones so vulnerable? How might a field of potatoes grown from seed, with variation, have fared differently?

check.q: Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
choices: A hen laying a fertilized egg
A pea flower fertilized by another pea plant
check.why: One bacterium splits into two identical cells with no mixing of genes.

check.q: A human egg cell carries how many chromosomes?
check.why: Egg and sperm each carry one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. Joined, they make 46.

check.q: What is the main advantage of sexual reproduction for a population?
choices: It is faster than asexual reproduction
It creates variation that helps some individuals survive changes
check.why: Mixing genes from two parents produces varied offspring, so some are likely to cope with new conditions.

lessons.title: The Punnett Square
lessons.mainIdea: A Punnett square lists every possible combination of alleles from two parents and shows how likely each one is.
reading: Around 1905, an English geneticist named Reginald Punnett drew a simple grid to keep track of Mendel's crosses. It is still used today. Write one parent's two alleles across the top and the other parent's two alleles down the side. Fill each box with one allele from the top and one from the side. The four boxes show every possible offspring.

Try a cross of two Rr plants. Across the top: R, r. Down the side: R, r. The boxes read RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Three boxes hold at least one R, so three quarters of the offspring are expected to be round. One box is rr, so one quarter are expected to be wrinkled. That is Mendel's three-to-one ratio drawn as a picture.

Now try Rr crossed with rr. The boxes read Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Half round, half wrinkled. The *Punnett square* does not tell you what any single seed will be. It tells you the chances. An organism with two identical alleles, like RR or rr, is *homozygous*. One with two different alleles, like Rr, is *heterozygous*. A heterozygous plant looks like a homozygous dominant one, but it carries the hidden allele.

words.d: a grid that shows all possible allele combinations from two parents and their chances
having two identical alleles for a gene, such as RR or rr
having two different alleles for a gene, such as Rr

look.title: The Cat Cross
look.text: In cats, a short coat is dominant over a long coat. A shelter has a short-haired mother cat that had one long-haired parent, so she carries one allele for each. The father is long-haired. Her litter has five kittens. Draw the grid before you answer.
look.prompt: What fraction of the kittens would you expect to have long hair? Could all five turn out short-haired? Explain.

check.q: In a Punnett square for Rr crossed with Rr, how many of the four boxes show the recessive trait?
check.why: Only the rr box shows the recessive trait; the other three contain a dominant R.

check.q: A plant with alleles Rr is called:
check.why: Two different alleles for one gene make an organism heterozygous.

check.q: Cross an Rr plant with an rr plant. What fraction of offspring is expected to be wrinkled?
check.why: The boxes are Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Two of four are rr, so half are expected to be wrinkled.

lessons.title: Chance, Not Certainty
lessons.mainIdea: Genetic ratios are probabilities; they describe many offspring on average, not what any single one must be.
reading: Flip a coin four times. You expect two heads, but you might get four, or none. Each flip is separate. Alleles work the same way. A Punnett square for Rr times Rr predicts one wrinkled seed in four. A single pod with six seeds might hold zero wrinkled seeds, or three. Only when you count thousands, as Mendel did, does the count settle close to the prediction.

This is why Mendel's numbers were 5,474 to 1,850, not exactly 5,475 to 1,825. *Probability* tells you the chance of each outcome, not the result of any one event. A couple who each carry one allele for a recessive condition has a one-in-four chance with each child. Having one child with the condition does not lower the chance for the next. Each fertilization is a new coin flip.

Understanding chance protects you from a common mistake. People sometimes say a trait "skipped a generation." It did not skip anything. A recessive allele was carried, hidden, by heterozygous parents. When two carriers happened to pass it on together, the trait appeared. Chance decided when, not any plan.

words.d: the chance that something will happen, often written as a fraction or percent
a heterozygous individual who carries a recessive allele without showing its trait

look.title: Two Pods
look.text: A student opens two pods from Rr plants. Pod 1 has seven seeds: five round, two wrinkled. Pod 2 has five seeds: all round. Her partner says the Punnett square must be wrong because neither pod shows a three-to-one ratio.
look.prompt: Is the partner right? What would you tell her about chance, and how many seeds would you want to count before judging the prediction?

check.q: Two carrier parents have a child with a recessive condition. The chance for their next child is:
check.why: Each fertilization is independent. The one-in-four chance is the same every time.

check.q: Why did Mendel need thousands of plants to see the three-to-one pattern clearly?
choices: Small samples vary a lot by chance; large ones settle near the expected ratio
Peas only show traits in big fields
He was paid by the plant
Small samples always show exactly three to one
check.why: Probability describes averages over many events, so large counts come closer to the prediction.

check.q: A trait seems to "skip a generation." What really happened?
choices: The gene disappeared and came back
The trait was caused by weather
The allele was not in the family until it was reinvented
A recessive allele was carried by heterozygous parents and then paired up
check.why: The allele never left. It was hidden in carriers until two copies met by chance in one offspring.

lessons.title: What a Mutation Is
lessons.mainIdea: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence, and it can come from copying mistakes or from damage by chemicals or radiation.
reading: Every time a cell divides, it copies about 3 billion base pairs. The copying machinery is remarkably accurate, and repair enzymes fix most slips, but a few errors get through. A single base may be swapped for another, dropped or added. Any change in the DNA sequence is a *mutation*. Ultraviolet light from the sun, some chemicals in tobacco smoke, and radiation can also damage DNA and cause mutations.

Where a mutation happens matters. A mutation in a skin cell affects only that cell and the cells that grow from it. It cannot be passed to children. A mutation in an egg or sperm cell can be passed on, and then every cell of the offspring will carry it. Mendel's wrinkled allele began, long ago, as a mutation in one pea plant that got passed down.

Most mutations change one letter among billions. Many land in stretches of DNA that do not code for any protein, so nothing happens. Others change one amino acid in a protein. Sometimes that makes no difference to the protein's shape. Sometimes it ruins it. Sometimes, rarely, it makes the protein work better in a new way. Mutations are the ultimate source of every new allele.

words.d: a change in the sequence of bases in DNA
energy such as ultraviolet light or X-rays that can damage DNA
the order of the bases along a strand of DNA

look.title: A Copying Slip
look.text: Imagine a sentence copied by hand a million times: THE CAT ATE THE RAT. In one copy the T in CAT became an H: THE CHAT ATE THE RAT. In another, a letter was dropped: THE CAT ATE TH RAT. In a third, a change landed in the blank space between words, and the sentence reads the same as before.
look.prompt: Match each copy to a kind of mutation: one that changes meaning, one that breaks meaning, and one that changes nothing. Why are all three still called mutations?

check.q: A mutation is:
choices: A change in the DNA sequence
Any change in an animal's behavior
A disease caused by a virus
check.why: Mutation means a change in the order of bases in DNA, whatever effect it has.

check.q: Which mutation could be passed on to a person's children?
choices: One in a sperm or egg cell
One caused by sunburn on the arm
check.why: Only mutations in the cells that form the next generation, egg and sperm, are inherited.

check.q: What happens to most single-letter mutations?
choices: They have little or no effect
check.why: Many land where they change nothing, or change a protein so slightly that it still works.

lessons.title: Harmful, Helpful, Neutral
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a mutation is harmful, helpful or neutral depends on what it does to a protein and on the environment the organism lives in.
reading: Consider one famous mutation. A single base change in the gene for hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, swaps one amino acid. With two copies of this allele, a person's red blood cells can bend into a stiff sickle shape, block small blood vessels and cause pain and organ damage. This is sickle cell disease. In that form, the mutation is clearly *harmful*.

Yet the same allele is common in parts of Africa, India and the Mediterranean where malaria is widespread. People with one sickle allele and one normal allele are mostly healthy, and they are much less likely to die of severe malaria. In a place with malaria, carrying one copy is *helpful*. In a place without it, the allele gives no benefit. Helpful and harmful are not fixed labels. They depend on the environment.

Another example is closer to lunch. Most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after infancy. Thousands of years ago, mutations arose in some human populations that keep the lactase gene switched on into adulthood. Where people herded cattle and drank milk, this allele spread. Where they did not, it stayed rare.

Most mutations are *neutral*: they change nothing you can measure. Your DNA differs from a classmate's at millions of positions, and nearly all of those differences have no effect at all. Neutral changes still matter to scientists. They pile up at a steady pace and can be used, like a clock, to estimate how long ago two populations or two species separated.

words.d: a mutation that makes an organism less likely to survive or reproduce in its environment
a mutation that makes an organism more likely to survive or reproduce in its environment
a mutation that has no measurable effect on the organism
the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen

look.title: Understanding Sickle Cell
look.text: Government health agencies explain that sickle cell disease is inherited, that a person must receive a sickle cell gene from both parents to have the disease, and that a person who receives the gene from only one parent has sickle cell trait, which usually causes no symptoms.
look.cite: U.S. National Institutes of Health and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, public health information, paraphrased
look.prompt: Using the words dominant, recessive and carrier, explain why a person with one sickle allele is usually healthy.

check.q: Why is the sickle cell allele common in regions with malaria?
choices: Having one copy protects against severe malaria
Malaria mosquitoes avoid people with two copies
check.why: Carriers survive malaria better, so the allele stays common even though two copies cause disease.

check.q: The same allele can be helpful in one place and useless in another. This shows that:
choices: Whether a mutation helps depends on the environment
Alleles change depending on the weather
check.why: A mutation's effect on survival depends on the conditions the organism faces.

check.q: Most differences between your DNA and a classmate's are:
check.why: Nearly all of the millions of differences between people have no measurable effect.

lessons.title: Selective Breeding
lessons.mainIdea: For thousands of years people have chosen which plants and animals reproduce, and that choice slowly reshapes a species.
reading: Drive through Illinois in August and you see corn to the horizon. Its ancestor was a wild grass from Mexico called teosinte, with tiny ears of a few hard kernels. Over thousands of years, farmers saved seed from the plants with the biggest, softest kernels and planted those. Generation by generation, the ears grew. This is *selective breeding*: humans choosing which individuals reproduce based on the traits they want.

Selective breeding does not create new alleles. It works on the variation that mutation and sexual reproduction already provide. A farmer cannot choose a trait that no plant in the field shows. But by breeding only the plants that lean the right way, the farmer makes the wanted alleles more common. Every dog breed, from Chihuahua to Great Dane, came from wolves this way. Cabbage, broccoli, kale and Brussels sprouts were all bred from one wild mustard plant.

There are trade-offs. Breeding for one trait can drag others along. Some dog breeds bred for a flat face struggle to breathe. Crop varieties bred for yield can lose disease resistance, which is why seed banks store older varieties. Illinois is home to a long-running corn experiment at the University of Illinois that has selected corn for high and low oil content every year since 1896, and the two lines still keep moving apart.

words.d: choosing which plants or animals reproduce so that wanted traits become more common
the wild grass from Mexico that farmers bred into corn
a group within a species, like a dog breed, shaped by selective breeding

look.title: Choosing the Seed
look.text: A gardener grows fifty tomato plants from the same seed packet. They vary: some fruits are sweet, some sour, some large, some small. She saves seed only from the three sweetest plants and grows those next year. She repeats this for ten years. By the end, nearly every plant is sweet, but the fruits are smaller and the plants get a leaf disease more often.
look.prompt: Explain how the gardener changed the tomatoes without adding any new alleles. What trade-off appeared, and why?

check.q: Selective breeding works by:
choices: Creating brand-new alleles in a lab
Letting only individuals with wanted traits reproduce
check.why: Breeders choose parents with the traits they want, making those alleles more common over generations.

check.q: Corn was bred from:
check.why: Farmers in Mexico slowly bred teosinte, a grass with tiny ears, into modern corn.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of selective breeding?
choices: It needs no variation to work

check.why: Selecting hard for one trait can drag along others, like breathing trouble in flat-faced dogs.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering
lessons.mainIdea: Genetic engineering moves or edits genes directly, which is faster and more precise than breeding and raises new questions.
reading: Before the 1980s, people with diabetes relied on insulin taken from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Then scientists cut the human insulin gene out of human DNA and pasted it into bacteria. The bacteria read the gene and built human insulin. It was approved for patients in 1982, and most insulin is made this way today. This is *genetic engineering*: changing an organism's DNA directly, often by adding a gene from another species.

Farmers use it too. Much of the corn grown in Illinois carries a gene from a soil bacterium that makes a protein toxic to certain caterpillars but not to people. Other crops carry genes that let them survive a weed killer. Newer tools such as CRISPR let scientists edit a gene in place, changing a few letters rather than adding a whole gene from elsewhere.

Genetic engineering is far faster than breeding and can move genes between species that could never breed. That power brings questions. Could an engineered gene spread to wild relatives? Are edited foods safe to eat? Who should own a gene? Scientists test engineered crops for years before approval, and the evidence so far shows approved foods are as safe as conventional ones, but debate about rules, labels and uses continues.

Compare the two methods with a pea plant. A breeder wanting a disease-resistant pea searches thousands of plants for one that resists, then crosses for years. An engineer finds the resistance gene, perhaps in a wild pea, and inserts it in one season. Both rely on the same fact: a gene is a recipe, and a cell will follow a recipe it is given.

words.d: changing an organism's DNA directly, often by adding or editing a gene
a protein hormone that controls blood sugar; people with diabetes may need to take it
a tool that lets scientists edit a gene in place inside a living cell

look.title: Two Paths to the Same Pea
look.text: A seed company wants a pea that resists a fungus. Team A screens 20,000 plants, finds three resistant ones, and crosses them with high-yield plants for six years until the resistance is stable. Team B finds the resistance gene in a wild pea and inserts it into the high-yield variety in one year. Team B's pea must then pass several years of safety tests before sale.
look.prompt: List one advantage and one drawback of each path. Why might a farmer or a shopper prefer one over the other?

choices: By bacteria carrying the human insulin gene
check.why: The human insulin gene was inserted into bacteria, which read it and build the protein.

check.q: What can genetic engineering do that selective breeding cannot?
choices: Move a gene between species that cannot breed together
check.why: Breeding only mixes alleles within a species. Engineering can add a gene from any organism.

choices: They are never tested before sale

check.why: Engineered crops go through years of safety testing, while questions about use and labeling are still discussed.

lessons.title: Reading the Whole Book
lessons.mainIdea: The Human Genome Project read the entire sequence of human DNA, giving scientists a map for finding genes linked to health and disease.
reading: In 1990 scientists in the United States and several other countries set out to read every base of human DNA, all 3 billion letters. The effort, called the Human Genome Project, took thirteen years and thousands of researchers. In 2003 they announced the sequence was essentially complete. A *genome* is an organism's entire set of DNA. Reading it is like getting the whole cookbook instead of one recipe.

The map surprised people. Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, far fewer than many had guessed, and about the same number as a mouse. Only a small fraction of the genome codes for proteins. Much of the rest controls when and where genes are switched on. Two unrelated people share about 99.9 percent of their sequence.

Since then, the cost of reading a genome has dropped from billions of dollars to a few hundred, and reading takes days instead of years. Doctors can now find the exact mutation behind some rare diseases in a child. Researchers compare genomes across species to trace how genes changed over time. The same map also raises questions about privacy and who may see your genetic information, questions that laws are still catching up with.

words.d: the complete set of DNA in an organism
the international effort, 1990 to 2003, to read the full sequence of human DNA
